### git merge-tree --write-tree

Source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge-tree/de.html

Performs a merge without touching the index or working tree, creating a new toplevel tree object. This is the modern mode of the command.

```APIDOC
## git merge-tree --write-tree

### Description
Performs a merge without touching the index or working tree, creating a new toplevel tree object. This is the modern mode of the command.

### Method
CLI

### Endpoint
_git merge-tree_ [--write-tree] [<options>] <branch1> <branch2>

### Parameters
#### Options
- **--stdin** - Optional - Read the commits to merge from standard input rather than the command-line. Implies -z.
- **-z** - Optional - Do not quote filenames in the Conflicted file info section, and end each filename with a NUL character rather than newline. Also begin the messages section with a NUL character instead of a newline.
- **--name-only** - Optional - In the Conflicted file info section, instead of writing a list of (mode, oid, stage, path) tuples, provide a list of filenames with conflicts.
- **--messages** - Optional - Write informational messages to the end of stdout. Default is to include messages if there are merge conflicts, and omit them otherwise.
- **--no-messages** - Optional - Do not write informational messages to stdout.
- **--quiet** - Optional - Disable all output from the program. Useful when only interested in the exit status.
- **--allow-unrelated-histories** - Optional - Override the check that errors out if the two branches share no common history.
- **--merge-base=<tree-ish>** - Optional - Specify a merge-base for the merge instead of finding them. Incompatible with --stdin.
- **-X<option>** - Optional - Pass a merge strategy-specific option through to the merge strategy.
- **--strategy-option=<option>** - Optional - Pass a merge strategy-specific option through to the merge strategy.

### Request Example
```
git merge-tree --write-tree <branch1> <branch2>
```

### Response
#### Success Response
- Creates a new toplevel tree object.
- Output details are described in the OUTPUT section of the documentation.

#### Response Example
(No explicit response example provided in the source.)
```

--------------------------------

### Shell script: Using git merge-tree in a series of steps

Source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge-tree/es.html

Shows a typical plumbing sequence using git merge-tree --write-tree to create a new tree, handle conflicts, and update a branch reference. Note that on non-zero exit status, NEWTREE contains more than just a tree.

```shell
vi message.txt
BRANCH1=refs/heads/test
BRANCH2=main
NEWTREE=$(git merge-tree --write-tree $BRANCH1 $BRANCH2) || {
    echo "There were conflicts..." 1>&2
    exit 1
}
NEWCOMMIT=$(git commit-tree $NEWTREE -F message.txt \
    -p $BRANCH1 -p $BRANCH2)
git update-ref $BRANCH1 $NEWCOMMIT
```

--------------------------------

### git merge-tree synopsis: --write-tree and --trivial-merge forms

Source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge-tree/es.html

Shows the two command-line forms of git merge-tree: the modern --write-tree mode and the deprecated --trivial-merge mode. The --write-tree form takes two branches, while the deprecated form takes a base tree and two branches.

```text
_git merge-tree_ [--write-tree] [<options>] <branch1> <branch2>
_git merge-tree_ [--trivial-merge] <base-tree> <branch1> <branch2> (deprecated)
```

--------------------------------

### Output for successful merge

Source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge-tree/es.html

For a successful merge, git-merge-tree outputs a single line containing the OID of the toplevel tree.

```text
<OID of toplevel tree>
```

### Merging multiple trees, continued

Source: https://git-scm.com/docs/user-manual/ja.html

Sadly, many merges aren’t trivial. If there are files that have been added, moved or removed, or if both branches have modified the same file, you will be left with an index tree that contains "merge entries" in it. Such an index tree can _NOT_ be written out to a tree object, and you will have to resolve any such merge clashes using other tools before you can write out the result.

You can examine such index state with `git` `ls-files` `--unmerged` command. An example:

```
$ git read-tree -m $orig HEAD $target
$ git ls-files --unmerged
100644 263414f423d0e4d70dae8fe53fa34614ff3e2860 1	hello.c
100644 06fa6a24256dc7e560efa5687fa84b51f0263c3a 2	hello.c
100644 cc44c73eb783565da5831b4d820c962954019b69 3	hello.c
```

Each line of the `git` `ls-files` `--unmerged` output begins with the blob mode bits, blob SHA-1, _stage number_ , and the filename. The _stage number_ is Git’s way to say which tree it came from: stage 1 corresponds to the `$orig` tree, stage 2 to the `HEAD` tree, and stage 3 to the `$target` tree.

Earlier we said that trivial merges are done inside `git` `read-tree` `-m`. For example, if the file did not change from `$orig` to `HEAD` or `$target`, or if the file changed from `$orig` to `HEAD` and `$orig` to `$target` the same way, obviously the final outcome is what is in `HEAD`. What the above example shows is that file `hello.c` was changed from `$orig` to `HEAD` and `$orig` to `$target` in a different way. You could resolve this by running your favorite 3-way merge program, e.g. `diff3`, `merge`, or Git’s own merge-file, on the blob objects from these three stages yourself, like this:

```
$ git cat-file blob 263414f >hello.c~1
$ git cat-file blob 06fa6a2 >hello.c~2
$ git cat-file blob cc44c73 >hello.c~3
$ git merge-file hello.c~2 hello.c~1 hello.c~3
```

This would leave the merge result in `hello.c~2` file, along with conflict markers if there are conflicts. After verifying the merge result makes sense, you can tell Git what the final merge result for this file is by:

```
$ mv -f hello.c~2 hello.c
$ git update-index hello.c
```

When a path is in the "unmerged" state, running `git` `update-index` for that path tells Git to mark the path resolved.

The above is the description of a Git merge at the lowest level, to help you understand what conceptually happens under the hood. In practice, nobody, not even Git itself, runs `git` `cat-file` three times for this. There is a `git` `merge-index` program that extracts the stages to temporary files and calls a "merge" script on it:

```
$ git merge-index git-merge-one-file hello.c
```

and that is what higher level `git` `merge` `-s` `resolve` is implemented with.
